name: Ahasuerus/Xerxes
title: Great King of Persia in the Book of Esther
summary: Ahasuerus, whom most scholars identify with the historical Xerxes I, was the great king of the Achaemenid (Persian) Empire and ruled over 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia. He is known from several biblical books, but above all from the book of Esther, where he is portrayed as a powerful yet impulsive and easily influenced ruler. After deposing his first queen Vashti, he chose the Jewish woman Esther as his new queen – without knowing her background. When his highest minister Haman received authority to issue a decree for the destruction of all Jews in the empire, Esther courageously stepped forward and exposed Haman's plan. The king reversed the situation: Haman was executed, Mordecai received his position, and the Jews were granted the right to defend themselves against their enemies. This dramatic deliverance is commemorated in the annual festival of Purim. Ahasuerus is also briefly mentioned in Ezra 4:6 in connection with accusations against the Jews in Jerusalem. Although God's name is never explicitly mentioned in the book of Esther, the course of the story testifies to God's hidden providence and faithful protection of His people in the diaspora.

keyEvents.title: The Grand Banquet
keyEvents.description: Ahasuerus held a magnificent banquet that lasted 180 days to display his wealth and splendor to all his princes and servants from the many provinces of the empire.

keyEvents.title: Queen Vashti's Refusal and Deposition
keyEvents.description: When Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command during the banquet, she was deposed as queen on the advice of the king's wise men. This opened the way for a new queen to be chosen.

keyEvents.title: Esther Becomes Queen
keyEvents.description: After an extensive search for a new queen, Ahasuerus chose Esther, a Jewish woman, and placed the royal crown on her head. A great banquet was held in her honor.

keyEvents.title: Mordecai Discovers the Assassination Plot
keyEvents.description: Mordecai discovered that two of the king's court officials, Bigthan and Teresh, were plotting to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. He informed Esther, who reported it to the king in Mordecai's name. The matter was investigated and found true, and the two men were hanged. The event was recorded in the king's chronicles.

keyEvents.title: Haman's Evil Plan
keyEvents.description: Haman persuaded the king that a certain people in the kingdom did not follow the king's laws, and obtained authority to issue a decree to destroy all Jews. The king gave Haman his signet ring without knowing that his own queen was Jewish.

keyEvents.title: Mordecai Honored
keyEvents.description: When the king had a sleepless night and ordered the chronicles to be read, he discovered that Mordecai had never been rewarded for exposing the assassination plot. He commanded Haman to honor Mordecai publicly through the city.

keyEvents.title: Esther's Revelation and Haman's Fall
keyEvents.description: During Esther's banquet, she revealed her Jewish identity and accused Haman of planning the destruction of her people. The king became furious, and Haman was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai.

keyEvents.title: The Deliverance of the Jews and the Institution of Purim
keyEvents.description: The king gave Mordecai Haman's position and signet ring. A new decree was issued granting the Jews the right to defend themselves against their enemies. The victory became the basis for the annual festival of Purim.

keyEvents.title: Accusation Against the Jews in Jerusalem
keyEvents.description: At the beginning of Ahasuerus' reign, opponents of the Jews sent a written accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem, attempting to halt the rebuilding work.

versions.summary: Ahasuerus, also known as Xerxes I, was king of the Persian Empire and ruled over 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia. He is best known from the Book of Esther, where he makes the Jewish woman Esther queen, and through her the Jewish people are saved from destruction. His reign marked a critical period for the Jews in exile.
versions.title: The mighty king of the Persian Empire
versions.reason: [minor] The Jews under Ahasuerus were not 'in exile' in the traditional sense. They were in the diaspora after many had already returned to Judah under Cyrus's decree. The phrasing 'the Jews in exile' is imprecise and should be adjusted to 'the Jews in the diaspora' or 'the Jews scattered throughout the Persian Empire'.; [major] Ahasuerus had more roles than just 'king'. He was also a military commander known for his campaign against Greece, and he was a lawgiver/administrator over a vast empire. The list should be expanded.; [minor] Ahasuerus also had Queen Vashti as his spouse before Esther. Although Esther is the most well-known, Vashti should be mentioned. Ideally, the spouse field should reflect both (but since the field accepts only one value, this can be addressed with a footnote).; [minor] Historically, Ahasuerus's (Xerxes I) mother was Atossa, daughter of Cyrus the Great. Although she is not directly mentioned in the Bible, this is well-documented historically and may be noted in a footnote.; [minor] Historically, Xerxes I had several children, including Artaxerxes I who succeeded him. Artaxerxes is mentioned in Ezra and Nehemiah. This should be included.; [minor] Mordecai's revelation of the assassination plot against the king (Est 2:21-23) is a significant event that lays the foundation for his later honor. It should be considered as its own key point.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. There is rich historical, archaeological, and linguistic data about Xerxes I that should be covered – including his identification with Xerxes I, Persian inscriptions, and the Persepolis palace.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew form 'Ahasuerus' (אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ, Aḥashverosh) is a rendering of the Old Persian Xšayāršā, which became Xerxes in Greek. Most scholars identify him with Xerxes I (486–465 BC), son of Darius I.

Archaeological findings from Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of Persia, confirm many details from the Book of Esther, including the grand palace architecture and banquet traditions. The reliefs from the Apadana hall show representatives from many nations of the empire bringing tribute, illustrating the extent of the kingdom as described in Est 1:1.

The administrative system of the Persian Empire with 127 provinces (Est 1:1) aligns with what we know about the satrapy system of the Achaemenid Empire. Herodotus and other Greek historians describe Xerxes' magnificent court and his famous invasion of Greece (480–479 BC), which likely took place between the events in Est 1 and Est 2.

Xerxes' mother Atossa was the daughter of Cyrus the Great and one of the most influential women in the Persian Empire. According to Herodotus, she played a decisive role in Xerxes being chosen as heir over his older brothers.

In Jewish tradition, Purim is celebrated annually to commemorate the deliverance of the Jews during Ahasuerus' reign. The Megillat Esther (Scroll of Esther) is read aloud in the synagogue, and the festival is marked by joy, gifts, and charity. The Talmud (Megilla 7a) discusses whether the Book of Esther was written under divine inspiration.

The Book of Esther is unique among biblical writings because God's name is never explicitly mentioned. Nevertheless, God's providence is clearly seen throughout the events—a theological point that has been widely discussed in both Jewish and Christian traditions. The book has received varying degrees of recognition in different Christian traditions, while it holds a very high status in Jewish tradition.

The Greek Septuagint version of the Book of Esther contains several additions that explicitly mention God by name, including prayers from Mordecai and Esther. These additions are considered deuterocanonical/apocryphal and are found in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, but not in the Hebrew canon.

Susa (Hebrew: Shushan), where most of the Book of Esther takes place, was one of the Persian capitals. French archaeologists have excavated the great palace at Susa and uncovered structures that correspond to the descriptions in Est 1:5–6, including a large garden attached to the palace.

Ahasuerus is also mentioned in Ezra 4:6, where it is reported that opponents of the Jews sent an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem at the beginning of his reign. This places him within the broader context of the Jewish people's return from exile and the rebuilding of Jerusalem.
